title: International education is one of Australia's largest exports, worth tens of billions of dollars a year
oneLiner: Fees and living expenses paid by overseas students rank with iron ore, coal and gas among export earners.
body: The Bureau of Statistics counts spending by international students as a service export. Through the 2010s it grew to be Australia's largest services export and one of the top four exports overall, and it underwrites a large share of university research funding.
contextBackground: The export framing is how the sector describes itself and how the national accounts record it. Critics note that much of the spending is on rent and goods that would otherwise be consumed locally, and that the net benefit is smaller than the gross figure.
contextDisagreement: The figure is accepted. Whether it represents a benefit to Australians or mainly to universities, and how much of it would be lost under a cap, is disputed.

claimItself.title: Net overseas migration should be held below 200,000 a year
claimItself.oneLiner: Whether the federal government should cap net arrivals below the levels of the past decade and well below the post-pandemic peak.
claimItself.body: Net overseas migration is arrivals minus departures of people who stay, or leave, for at least twelve months. It averaged just over 200,000 a year in the decade before the pandemic and exceeded 500,000 in 2022–23. The proposal is a cap of 200,000, which would require the government to manage the student, temporary-work and permanent programs together to hit it.

claimItself.title: Holding net overseas migration below 200,000 would require large cuts to international student numbers
claimItself.oneLiner: Students are the biggest component of net migration, so a cap of this size is mostly a cap on them.
claimItself.body: Permanent skilled and family visas are already capped and make up a minority of net migration. The remainder is dominated by students, with working-holiday makers and temporary skilled workers behind them. Holding the total below 200,000 while keeping the permanent program at current levels leaves international education as the only component large enough to cut.
